import { VINTAGE_18000 } from "./catalog/vintage18000";
import { readWatch, ZERO_SETTINGS, POSITIONS, type WatchSettings, type WatchReading, type WatchSpec } from "./core/watch";
import { nominalPeriod } from "./core/oscillator/period";
import { initialPose, step, type EscapementPose, type Phase } from "./core/escapement/kinematics";
import { shapes, stonePenetration } from "./core/escapement/shapes";
import { derived } from "./core/escapement/params";
import { CONTACT_TOL } from "./core/escapement/kinematics";
import { analyze, type Reading } from "./core/timegrapher/analyze";
import { advanceTicks, emptyWindow, type TickWindow } from "./app/ticker";
import { renderMovement } from "./view/movement";
import { renderTimegrapher } from "./view/timegrapher";
import { PUZZLES, type Puzzle } from "./puzzles";
import { STATES } from "./verify/states";

const calibre = VINTAGE_18000;
const esc = calibre.escapement;
const T = nominalPeriod(calibre.beatRate);
const TRACE_BEATS = 300;
/** Timegrapher clock runs this many times faster than the wall clock (decision: two clocks). */
const SIM_SPEEDUP = 10;

// ---------- state ----------
let puzzle: Puzzle | null = PUZZLES[0];
let user: WatchSettings = { ...ZERO_SETTINGS };
let animSpeed = 1;
let animPaused = false;
let animTime = T / 4;
let simTime = 0;
let win: TickWindow = emptyWindow();
let pose: EscapementPose = initialPose(esc, 0);
let reading: WatchReading = readWatch(calibre.watch, user);
let tg: Reading | null = null;
let heldSeconds = 0;
let solved = false;
let answered: number | null = null;
let lastWall = performance.now();

const spec = (): WatchSpec => (puzzle?.specOverride ? puzzle.specOverride(calibre.watch) : calibre.watch);
const effective = (): WatchSettings => {
  const f = puzzle?.faults ?? {};
  return {
    ...user,
    regulatorIndex: user.regulatorIndex + (f.regulatorIndex ?? 0),
    beatOffsetDeg: user.beatOffsetDeg + (f.beatOffsetDeg ?? 0),
    unbalance: user.unbalance + (f.unbalance ?? 0),
    heavySpotDeg: f.heavySpotDeg ?? user.heavySpotDeg,
    inertiaTrim: user.inertiaTrim,
  };
};

// ---------- DOM ----------
const $ = <T extends HTMLElement>(id: string) => document.getElementById(id) as T;
const movementEl = $("movement"), tgEl = $("timegrapher"), puzzleEl = $("puzzle");

function balanceAngleAt(t: number) {
  return reading.running ? reading.amplitudeDeg * Math.sin((2 * Math.PI * t) / reading.period) - reading.beatOffsetDeg : -reading.beatOffsetDeg;
}

function recompute() {
  reading = readWatch(spec(), effective());
}

function drawMovement() {
  movementEl.innerHTML = renderMovement(esc, pose, animTime * 1000);
  if (!reading.running) movementEl.querySelector(".phase")!.textContent = "STOPPED · no torque at the escape wheel";
}
function drawTimegrapher() {
  tgEl.innerHTML = renderTimegrapher({ reading: tg, nominalPeriod: T, liftAngle: calibre.liftAngle, running: reading.running, knocking: reading.knocking, spanSeconds: (TRACE_BEATS * T) / 2, speedup: SIM_SPEEDUP });
}
function drawPuzzle() {
  if (!puzzle) { puzzleEl.innerHTML = `<h2>Free play</h2><p>Adjust anything. The timegrapher shows what a watchmaker would see.</p>`; return; }
  const idx = PUZZLES.indexOf(puzzle);
  puzzleEl.innerHTML = `<h2>Puzzle ${idx + 1} · ${puzzle.title}</h2>
    <p class="symptom">${puzzle.symptom}</p>
    <p class="goal"><strong>Goal:</strong> ${puzzle.goal}</p>
    ${Number.isFinite(puzzle.holdSeconds) ? `<div class="hold"><div class="bar" style="width:${Math.min(100, (100 * heldSeconds) / puzzle.holdSeconds).toFixed(1)}%"></div><span>${solved ? "solved" : `${heldSeconds.toFixed(0)} / ${puzzle.holdSeconds} s in band`}</span></div>` : ""}
    ${puzzle.question ? `<div class="question"><p>${puzzle.question.prompt}</p>${puzzle.question.choices.map((c, i) => `<button class="choice ${answered === i ? (i === puzzle!.question!.correct ? "right" : "wrong") : ""}" data-choice="${i}">${c}</button>`).join("")}${answered !== null ? `<p class="verdict">${answered === puzzle.question.correct ? puzzle.question.whyCorrect : "Not quite. Watch the rate as the wind runs down, then try again."}</p>` : ""}</div>` : ""}
    ${solved ? `<details open><summary>Why it worked</summary><p>${puzzle.explanation}</p></details>` : ""}`;
  puzzleEl.querySelectorAll<HTMLButtonElement>(".choice").forEach((b) => (b.onclick = () => { answered = Number(b.dataset.choice); if (answered === puzzle!.question!.correct) solved = true; drawPuzzle(); }));
}
function drawControls() {
  const show = (name: string) => !puzzle || puzzle.controls.includes(name as never) || puzzle.controls.length === 0;
  for (const name of ["regulator", "beat", "wind", "screws", "position"]) $(`ctl-${name}`).hidden = !show(name);
  $("ctl-poise").hidden = $("ctl-poise-angle").hidden = !show("poise");
  $("readout-rate").textContent = reading.running ? `${reading.rateSecondsPerDay >= 0 ? "+" : "−"}${Math.abs(reading.rateSecondsPerDay).toFixed(1)} s/day true rate` : "stopped";
}

// ---------- frame loop ----------
function frame(now: number) {
  const wallDt = Math.min(0.1, (now - lastWall) / 1000);
  lastWall = now;
  if (!animPaused) {
    const dt = wallDt * animSpeed;
    animTime += dt;
    pose = step(esc, pose, balanceAngleAt(animTime), Math.max(dt, 1e-6));
    drawMovement();
  }
  // Timegrapher clock.
  const simDt = wallDt * SIM_SPEEDUP;
  simTime += simDt;
  win = advanceTicks(win, reading, simTime, TRACE_BEATS);
  tg = analyze(win.ticks, T, calibre.liftAngle);
  drawTimegrapher();
  if (puzzle && !solved && Number.isFinite(puzzle.holdSeconds)) {
    heldSeconds = puzzle.band(reading, tg) ? heldSeconds + simDt : 0;
    if (heldSeconds >= puzzle.holdSeconds) solved = true;
    drawPuzzle();
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}

// ---------- controls ----------
// Poising control: built here (not in index.html) because it arrived after the layout was handed to design.
{
  const footer = document.querySelector("footer")!;
  const anchor = $("ctl-position");
  const mk = (id: string, label: string, min: number, max: number, step: number) => {
    const l = document.createElement("label"); l.id = `ctl-${id}`;
    l.innerHTML = `${label} <input id="${id}" type="range" min="${min}" max="${max}" step="${step}" value="0" /><span class="value" id="${id}-value"></span>`;
    footer.insertBefore(l, anchor);
  };
  mk("poise", "Poising: remove weight (µg·cm)", 0, 15, 0.25);
  mk("poise-angle", "Poising: at rim position (°)", 0, 360, 5);
  const wrap = document.createElement("div"); wrap.id = "ctl-poise-group"; // keep hide/show simple
  footer.insertBefore(wrap, anchor);
  wrap.append($("ctl-poise"), $("ctl-poise-angle"));
  wrap.style.display = "contents";
}
function bindRange(id: string, key: keyof WatchSettings, fmt: (v: number) => string) {
  const el = $<HTMLInputElement>(id), out = $(`${id}-value`);
  const apply = () => { (user as any)[key] = Number(el.value); out.textContent = fmt(Number(el.value)); recompute(); drawControls(); };
  el.oninput = apply; apply();
}
bindRange("regulator", "regulatorIndex", (v) => `${v >= 0 ? "+" : "−"}${Math.abs(v).toFixed(2)}° ${v > 0 ? "(toward F)" : v < 0 ? "(toward S)" : ""}`);
bindRange("beat", "beatOffsetDeg", (v) => `${v.toFixed(1)}°`);
bindRange("wind", "hoursSinceWind", (v) => `${v.toFixed(0)} h since wound`);
bindRange("screws", "inertiaTrim", (v) => `${(v * 100).toFixed(2)} % inertia`);
{
  const amt = $<HTMLInputElement>("poise"), ang = $<HTMLInputElement>("poise-angle");
  const apply = () => {
    user.poiseCorrection = Number(amt.value) * 1e-11; user.poiseCorrectionDeg = Number(ang.value);
    $("poise-value").textContent = `${Number(amt.value).toFixed(2)} µg·cm`; $("poise-angle-value").textContent = `${ang.value}° on the rim`;
    recompute(); drawControls();
  };
  amt.oninput = apply; ang.oninput = apply; apply();
}
$<HTMLSelectElement>("position").onchange = (e) => { user.position = (e.target as HTMLSelectElement).value as WatchSettings["position"]; recompute(); drawControls(); };
$<HTMLSelectElement>("position").innerHTML = POSITIONS.map((p) => `<option value="${p.id}">${p.label}</option>`).join("");
$<HTMLSelectElement>("speed").onchange = (e) => { animSpeed = Number((e.target as HTMLSelectElement).value); };
$("pause").onclick = () => { animPaused = !animPaused; $("pause").textContent = animPaused ? "Play" : "Pause"; };
const puzzleSel = $<HTMLSelectElement>("puzzle-select");
puzzleSel.innerHTML = `<option value="">Free play</option>` + PUZZLES.map((p, i) => `<option value="${p.id}">Puzzle ${i + 1}: ${p.title}</option>`).join("");
function loadPuzzle(id: string | null) {
  puzzle = PUZZLES.find((p) => p.id === id) ?? null;
  puzzleSel.value = puzzle?.id ?? "";
  user = { ...ZERO_SETTINGS };
  for (const id of ["regulator", "beat", "wind", "screws", "poise", "poise-angle"]) { $<HTMLInputElement>(id).value = "0"; }
  $<HTMLSelectElement>("position").value = "DU";
  heldSeconds = 0; solved = false; answered = null; win = emptyWindow(); simTime = 0;
  recompute(); drawControls(); drawPuzzle();
  for (const id of ["regulator", "beat", "wind", "screws", "poise", "poise-angle"]) $<HTMLInputElement>(id).dispatchEvent(new Event("input"));
}
puzzleSel.onchange = () => loadPuzzle(puzzleSel.value || null);
$("calibre-name").textContent = calibre.name;

// ---------- verify-render contract ----------
const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
let named: string | null = null;
function timeForPhase(phase: Phase, beat: 0 | 1, frac: number): number {
  // Scan one period from T/4 with a fresh pose, find the phase window on the requested beat.
  const N = 4000;
  let p = initialPose(esc, balanceAngleAt(T / 4));
  let t = T / 4, start: number | null = null, found: [number, number] | null = null, beatIdx = -1, lastPhase: Phase = p.phase;
  for (let i = 1; i <= N && !found; i++) {
    const nt = T / 4 + (i / N) * T;
    p = step(esc, p, balanceAngleAt(nt), nt - t); t = nt;
    if (p.phase === "unlock" && lastPhase === "lock") beatIdx++;
    if (beatIdx === beat && p.phase === phase && start === null) start = t;
    if (start !== null && p.phase !== phase) found = [start, t];
    lastPhase = p.phase;
  }
  return found ? found[0] + frac * (found[1] - found[0]) : T / 4;
}
if (q.has("state") && STATES[q.get("state")!]) {
  named = q.get("state")!;
  const s = STATES[named];
  loadPuzzle(s.puzzle);
  Object.assign(user, s.settings);
  recompute();
  // Accumulate ticks for the requested sim span, then freeze everything.
  win = advanceTicks(win, reading, s.simSeconds, TRACE_BEATS);
  simTime = s.simSeconds;
  tg = analyze(win.ticks, T, calibre.liftAngle);
  animPaused = true;
  animTime = T / 4;
  pose = initialPose(esc, balanceAngleAt(T / 4));
  if (s.freeze) {
    animTime = timeForPhase(s.freeze.phase, s.freeze.beat, s.freeze.frac ?? 0.5);
    let t = T / 4;
    while (t < animTime) { const nt = Math.min(animTime, t + 1e-4); pose = step(esc, pose, balanceAngleAt(nt), nt - t); t = nt; }
  }
  drawMovement(); drawTimegrapher(); drawPuzzle(); drawControls();
  movementEl.querySelector("svg")!.setAttribute("data-state", named);
}
(window as any).__bench = {
  states: () => Object.keys(STATES),
  describe: () => (named ? STATES[named].describe : "free-running"),
  check: () => {
    if (!named) return [];
    const e = STATES[named].expect;
    const out: { name: string; pass: boolean; detail: string }[] = [];
    const g = shapes(esc, pose);
    let worst = -Infinity;
    for (const tooth of g.teeth) for (const st of [g.entryStone, g.exitStone]) worst = Math.max(worst, stonePenetration(tooth, st));
    out.push({ name: "no tooth inside a stone", pass: worst <= CONTACT_TOL * 1.01, detail: `max penetration ${worst.toExponential(2)}` });
    out.push({ name: "lever within bankings", pass: Math.abs(pose.forkAngle) <= derived(esc).forkHalf + 1e-9, detail: `fork ${pose.forkAngle.toFixed(3)}°` });
    if (e.phase) out.push({ name: "escapement phase", pass: pose.phase === e.phase, detail: `got ${pose.phase}, expected ${e.phase}` });
    if (e.running !== undefined) out.push({ name: "running", pass: reading.running === e.running, detail: `running=${reading.running}` });
    if (e.rateWithin && tg) out.push({ name: "timegrapher rate", pass: tg.rateSecondsPerDay >= e.rateWithin[0] && tg.rateSecondsPerDay <= e.rateWithin[1], detail: `${tg.rateSecondsPerDay.toFixed(1)} s/day, expected ${e.rateWithin.join("..")}` });
    if (e.amplitudeWithin && tg) out.push({ name: "timegrapher amplitude", pass: tg.amplitudeDeg >= e.amplitudeWithin[0] && tg.amplitudeDeg <= e.amplitudeWithin[1], detail: `${tg.amplitudeDeg.toFixed(1)}°, expected ${e.amplitudeWithin.join("..")}` });
    if (e.beatErrorBelow !== undefined && tg) out.push({ name: "beat error", pass: tg.beatErrorMs < e.beatErrorBelow, detail: `${tg.beatErrorMs.toFixed(2)} ms` });
    out.push({ name: "instrument agrees with physics on rate", pass: !tg || !reading.running || Math.abs(tg.rateSecondsPerDay - reading.rateSecondsPerDay) < 0.5, detail: `instrument ${tg?.rateSecondsPerDay.toFixed(2)} vs true ${reading.rateSecondsPerDay.toFixed(2)}` });
    return out;
  },
};

if (!named) { loadPuzzle(PUZZLES[0].id); pose = initialPose(esc, balanceAngleAt(animTime)); drawMovement(); drawTimegrapher(); }
requestAnimationFrame(frame);

/** Named states for the verify-render skill. Each sets puzzle, settings and animation phase. */
import type { WatchSettings } from "../core/watch";
import type { Phase } from "../core/escapement/kinematics";

export interface NamedState {
  describe: string;
  puzzle: string | null;
  settings: Partial<WatchSettings>;
  /** Freeze the animation at the middle of this escapement phase on this beat (0 entry, 1 exit). */
  freeze?: { phase: Phase; beat: 0 | 1; frac?: number };
  /** Simulated seconds of ticks to accumulate before the shot. */
  simSeconds: number;
  expect: { phase?: Phase; rateWithin?: [number, number]; amplitudeWithin?: [number, number]; beatErrorBelow?: number; running?: boolean };
}

export const STATES: Record<string, NamedState> = {
  "healthy-full-wind": { describe: "Free play, no puzzle: healthy watch, dial up, full wind. Trace flat, two lines overlapping, ~280°.", puzzle: null, settings: {}, simSeconds: 120, expect: { rateWithin: [-1, 1], amplitudeWithin: [275, 285], beatErrorBelow: 0.1, running: true } },
  "runs-fast-start": { describe: "Puzzle 1 as loaded: trace sloping (ticks early), readout about +40 s/day.", puzzle: "runs-fast", settings: {}, simSeconds: 120, expect: { rateWithin: [35, 45], running: true } },
  "runs-fast-fixed": { describe: "Puzzle 1 with the regulator moved 1.2° toward Slow: trace flat, rate near 0.", puzzle: "runs-fast", settings: { regulatorIndex: -1.2 }, simSeconds: 120, expect: { rateWithin: [-3, 3], running: true } },
  "out-of-beat": { describe: "Puzzle 2 as loaded: two trace lines clearly separated, beat error well above 0.5 ms.", puzzle: "out-of-beat", settings: {}, simSeconds: 120, expect: { running: true } },
  "slump-evening": { describe: "Puzzle 3 at 24 h of wind: amplitude near 200°, watch gaining a few s/day.", puzzle: "afternoon-slump", settings: { hoursSinceWind: 24 }, simSeconds: 120, expect: { amplitudeWithin: [190, 210], rateWithin: [2, 15], running: true } },
  // Heavy spot at the bottom when crown up; at 250° (above the 219.5° crossover) that is a LOSS. See docs/research/04.
  "position-crown-up": { describe: "Puzzle 4 crown up: amplitude ~250°, heavy spot at the bottom, poise error showing as a loss of several s/day.", puzzle: "position-error", settings: { position: "CU" }, simSeconds: 120, expect: { amplitudeWithin: [245, 255], rateWithin: [-15, -2], running: true } },
  "position-crown-down": { describe: "Puzzle 4 crown down: same amplitude, heavy spot now at the top, poise error a gain.", puzzle: "position-error", settings: { position: "CD" }, simSeconds: 120, expect: { amplitudeWithin: [245, 255], rateWithin: [2, 15], running: true } },
  "position-poised": { describe: "Puzzle 4 crown up after removing 10 µg·cm at 0°: rate back near zero.", puzzle: "position-error", settings: { position: "CU", poiseCorrection: 10e-11, poiseCorrectionDeg: 0 }, simSeconds: 120, expect: { rateWithin: [-2, 2], running: true } },
  "stopped": { describe: "Healthy watch at 42 h: no signal, balance still, readouts blank.", puzzle: null, settings: { hoursSinceWind: 42 }, simSeconds: 60, expect: { running: false } },
  "entry-impulse": { describe: "Movement frozen mid entry impulse: pin in notch, tooth on the entry impulse face.", puzzle: null, settings: {}, freeze: { phase: "impulse", beat: 0 }, simSeconds: 10, expect: { phase: "impulse" } },
  "exit-lock": { describe: "Movement frozen at exit lock: pin far from notch, tooth resting on the exit locking face.", puzzle: null, settings: {}, freeze: { phase: "lock", beat: 1 }, simSeconds: 10, expect: { phase: "lock" } },
};

# Glossary

Terms used in code, tests and docs. Identifiers use these words, not synonyms. Entries marked
*(spike)* are already encoded in `spike/`; the rest enter the vocabulary when the core is built.
Physics claims behind them are checked in `docs/research/`.

## Oscillator

- **balance** — the oscillating wheel. Its angle from rest is `balanceAngle` (degrees). *(spike)*
- **hairspring** — the spiral spring returning the balance to rest. Its stiffness sets the period together with balance inertia.
- **amplitude** — peak balance angle from rest, degrees. Healthy at full wind: roughly 250–300° dial up. *(spike, as `balanceAmplitude`)*
- **beat** — one half-swing of the balance, from one extreme to the other. One tick. *(spike)*
- **beat rate** — beats per hour (bph). 18,000 bph = 5 beats/s = 0.4 s period. *(spike)*
- **period** — time for a full swing (two beats). *(spike)*
- **regulator index** — the lever that slides the curb pins along the hairspring, changing its active length and so the rate. Marked F/S or +/−.
- **timing screws** — screws on the balance rim; turning them in or out changes balance inertia and so the rate.
- **stud** — the fixed outer anchor of the hairspring. Rotating the stud carrier changes where the balance rests relative to the fork: the **beat adjustment**.
- **poise** — the balance's mass balance about its axis. A **poise error** (heavy spot) changes rate in vertical positions.
- **isochronism** — the property of keeping the same period at any amplitude. Its absence is **isochronism error**.

## Escapement

- **escape wheel** — the toothed wheel the gear train drives; released one half-tooth per beat. `wheelAngle` is degrees of rotation in the direction of tooth travel. *(spike)*
- **tooth pitch** — 360° / tooth count. 24° for 15 teeth. *(spike)*
- **pallet fork** (lever) — the pivoted piece carrying two pallet stones and the notch. Its angle from centre is `forkAngle`. *(spike)*
- **pallet stone** (pallet) — the jewel that stops and then pushes the escape wheel. **Entry** stone meets each tooth first; **exit** stone last. *(spike)*
- **locking face** — the stone face a tooth rests on while the wheel is stopped. *(spike)*
- **impulse face** — the inclined stone face a tooth slides along, pushing the fork. *(spike)*
- **locking corner** — where the two faces meet. **Let-off corner** — the far end of the impulse face, where the tooth leaves. *(spike)*
- **lock** — the phase with the tooth at rest on a locking face. `lockAngle` is the lever rotation needed to unlock. *(spike)*
- **unlock** — the lever lifting a stone until the tooth tip passes the locking corner. *(spike)*
- **impulse** — the tooth sliding along an impulse face and pushing the fork, which pushes the balance. `liftLever` is the lever rotation it spans. *(spike)*
- **drop** — the escape wheel in free flight between leaving one stone and landing on the other. `drop` is the wheel rotation it spans. *(spike)*
- **run to banking** — the lever's remaining travel after drop until it rests on a banking pin. *(spike)*
- **banking** — the pins that limit lever travel; the lever rests on one between beats. *(spike)*
- **draw** — an angle (12–15° in practice) on the locking face so the wheel's torque pulls the lever onto its banking and recoils the wheel slightly during unlock. Zero in the drawing; its energy cost is a loss term in the oscillator model.
- **ratchet tooth / club tooth** — pointed teeth (English lever, all lift on the pallet) versus teeth with their own impulse face (Swiss, lift split roughly 3° tooth : 5.5° pallet). The drawing uses ratchet teeth on a Swiss in-line layout; UI copy says "lever escapement".
- **impulse pin** (roller jewel) — the pin on the balance that enters the fork's **notch** each beat. *(spike)*
- **lift angle** — the balance's travel while the impulse pin is in the notch. Timegraphers assume it (52° default) to compute amplitude. *(spike, as `liftAngle`)*
- **tangential geometry** — the layout rule placing the fork pivot where lines tangent to the escape wheel meet, with the stones at the tangent points. *(spike)*
- **circular / equidistant pallets** — two conventions for where the entry and exit lock arcs sit; the choice makes the two impulses asymmetric. The spike is circular.

## Instrument

- **timegrapher** — the bench instrument that listens to the ticks and reports rate, amplitude and beat error.
- **rate** — gain or loss in seconds per day (s/day). Positive = fast.
- **beat error** — the difference in milliseconds between tick-to-tock and tock-to-tick intervals. Zero means the balance rests centred.
- **trace** — the timegrapher's dotted plot of tick timing against beat number: slope is rate, separation of the two lines is beat error.

## Power

- **mainspring** — the coiled spring that stores energy. Its **torque curve** falls as it unwinds, lowering amplitude.
- **state of wind** — how much of the mainspring's run time remains.
- **gear train** — the wheels between mainspring and escape wheel; simplified in the drawing.

## Bench

- **calibre** — a named movement; one parameter set in the watch catalog.
- **position** — the watch's orientation (dial up, crown down, …) during timing.
- **puzzle** — a bundled faulty calibre with a symptom, a hidden cause and a completion rule.

# Judgment log

Moments where Claude asserted wrong horology, a test was restated, or a render ran but looked
wrong, and the correction. Kept for the design doc; the brief rewards these being visible.

| When | What Claude did | How it was caught | Correction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spike, round 1 | Built the pallet locking face radial to the escape wheel | Invariant tests: wheel crept while locked, beats asymmetric | Face is an arc about the fork pivot (zero draw); later an exact region, not a polygon |
| Spike, round 2 | Diagnosed the failure as polygon non-convexity | Tests unchanged after the fix | Wrong diagnosis; recorded as a wasted round |
| Spike, round 7 | Reported a false "drop" mid-impulse | Phase trace showed the wheel losing contact before the let-off | Free-run speed was below the face's recession rate; raised it |
| Spike, tests | Wrote "half a tooth per beat from any instant" and "stationary while locked" including run-to-banking | Both failed on real geometry | Restated as lock-to-lock and pin-out-of-notch; the original wording encoded a false symmetry. Akash to confirm these are restatements, not loosenings |
| Spike, render 1 | Stones drawn as a sliver and a sail, lever tail into the wheel, bankings misplaced | Screenshots read with the verify-render loop | Outline now derived from the same region used for collision |
| Research brief | Claude told the isochronism agent that a lever watch gains at low amplitude *because the impulse is mostly an advance* | The agent read Airy (1826), Hoyng (2015) and patent US 9,323,223: the escapement alone is a loss that grows at low amplitude; the net gain in flat-spring watches comes from the regulator pins | Model split into an escapement loss term and a pin gain term; puzzle 3 text says "the escapement alone would make it lose" |
| Research brief | The brief's "280° → 200° after a day" was taken as a healthy watch | Witschi and bench reports: healthy is a 10–15 % drop; 200° at 24 h is a tired spring | Healthy curve 280° → 250°; the slump puzzle uses a tired-spring torque curve |
| App, first render | Timegrapher states showed "LOCK" with the pin inside the notch | Screenshot review: an impossible pose | Movement parks at a true lock before freezing; `initialPose` only reports lock when actually blocked |
| App, first render | Beat error of 2.7 ms invisible on a ±100 ms trace scale | Screenshot review | Scale ±20 ms with wrapping, like a real machine |
| App, first build | Puzzle 2's completion rule never looked at beat error | Hold bar started filling the moment the puzzle loaded | Bands receive the instrument reading as well as the physics |
| App, first build | 60× sim clock made the 60-second hold finish in one wall second | Reasoning about the rule, not a screenshot | 10×, recorded in CLAUDE.md |
| App, puzzle 4 states | Claude wrote the expectation "crown up gains" for a heavy spot at the bottom | verify-render: the model lost 6 s/day; research 04 says above 219.5° a bottom heavy spot loses | Expectation corrected; the model was right |

/** Timegrapher panel: trace plus readouts. Reads a Reading; computes nothing but pixels. */
import type { Reading } from "../core/timegrapher/analyze";

export interface TimegrapherView {
  reading: Reading | null;
  nominalPeriod: number;
  liftAngle: number;
  running: boolean;
  knocking: boolean;
  /** Sim seconds the trace spans, for the honest label. */
  spanSeconds: number;
  /** Sim seconds per wall second, for the honest label. */
  speedup: number;
}

const fmt = (x: number, d: number) => (Math.abs(x) < 0.5 * 10 ** -d ? "" : x > 0 ? "+" : "−") + Math.abs(x).toFixed(d);

export function renderTimegrapher(v: TimegrapherView): string {
  const W = 420, H = 300, pad = 36;
  const beatMs = (v.nominalPeriod / 2) * 1000;
  const yRange = Math.min(20, beatMs / 2); // ±20 ms, wrapping like a real machine's screen
  const r = v.reading;
  const dots = r
    ? r.trace.map((p) => {
        const x = pad + ((W - 2 * pad) * p.beat) / Math.max(1, r.trace.length - 1);
        let off = ((p.offsetMs + yRange) % (2 * yRange) + 2 * yRange) % (2 * yRange) - yRange; // wrap
        const y = H / 2 - (off / yRange) * (H / 2 - pad);
        return `<circle class="dot p${p.parity}" cx="${x.toFixed(1)}" cy="${y.toFixed(1)}" r="1.5"/>`;
      }).join("")
    : "";
  const rate = r && v.running ? fmt(r.rateSecondsPerDay, 0) : "—";
  const amp = r && v.running ? r.amplitudeDeg.toFixed(0) : "—";
  const be = r && v.running ? r.beatErrorMs.toFixed(1) : "—";
  // Faint horizontal grid at ±10 ms: half the screen range, purely a reading aid.
  const gridY = [H / 2 - (H / 2 - pad) / 2, H / 2 + (H / 2 - pad) / 2];
  return `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H + 84}" class="timegrapher" data-rate="${r?.rateSecondsPerDay ?? ""}">
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="${W}" height="${H}" rx="2" class="screen"/>
  <rect x="0.5" y="0.5" width="${W - 1}" height="${H - 1}" rx="2" class="screen-edge"/>
  ${gridY.map((y) => `<line x1="${pad}" y1="${y}" x2="${W - pad}" y2="${y}" class="grid"/>`).join("")}
  <line x1="${pad}" y1="${H / 2}" x2="${W - pad}" y2="${H / 2}" class="axis"/>
  <text x="${pad}" y="${pad - 10}" class="axislabel">+${yRange.toFixed(0)} ms</text>
  <text x="${pad}" y="${H - pad + 18}" class="axislabel">−${yRange.toFixed(0)} ms</text>
  <text x="${W - pad}" y="${H - pad + 18}" class="axislabel" text-anchor="end">${v.spanSeconds.toFixed(0)} s of ticks at ${v.speedup}× time</text>
  ${v.knocking ? `<text x="${W / 2}" y="${H / 2}" class="warn" text-anchor="middle">Knocking: amplitude unreliable</text>` : ""}
  ${v.running ? dots : `<text x="${W / 2}" y="${H / 2}" class="warn" text-anchor="middle">No signal. The watch has stopped.</text>`}
  <g class="readouts" transform="translate(0,${H + 10})">
    <line x1="${W / 3}" y1="8" x2="${W / 3}" y2="56" class="divider"/>
    <line x1="${2 * W / 3}" y1="8" x2="${2 * W / 3}" y2="56" class="divider"/>
    <text x="${pad}" y="34" class="big">${rate}<tspan class="unit"> s/day</tspan></text>
    <text x="${W / 2}" y="34" class="big" text-anchor="middle">${amp}<tspan class="unit">°</tspan></text>
    <text x="${W - pad}" y="34" class="big" text-anchor="end">${be}<tspan class="unit"> ms</tspan></text>
    <text x="${pad}" y="56" class="small">rate</text>
    <text x="${W / 2}" y="56" class="small" text-anchor="middle">amplitude at ${v.liftAngle}° lift angle</text>
    <text x="${W - pad}" y="56" class="small" text-anchor="end">beat error</text>
  </g>
</svg>`;
}

name: verify-render
description: Verify that the movement renders correctly. Use after any change to shapes, the renderer, the sim core, or a named state, before saying a visual is done, and when a user reports a render that looks wrong. Screenshots named states via Playwright and runs numeric geometry checks the page exposes.
---

# verify-render

Vision alone misses fine geometry. This skill pairs screenshots with numbers: the page exposes
named states and a `check()` that returns pass/fail assertions computed from the same shapes
the renderer draws. The script drives both and reports like a test run.

## Contract the app must honour

- `?state=<name>` in the URL loads a named state, paused.
- `window.__bench` exists after render with:
  - `states(): string[]` — every named state.
  - `check(): { name: string; pass: boolean; detail: string }[]` — numeric assertions for the
    state currently shown (no overlap, contact on the expected face, lever within bankings,
    anything the state declares it expects).
  - `describe(): string` — one line: what this state is supposed to show.
- The root `<svg>` carries `data-state="<name>"` once rendered.

Named states and their expectations live in `src/verify/states.ts` (root app) or
`spike/src/states.ts` (spike). A new visual feature adds a state there; it never adds a check
to the renderer.

## Steps

1. Run the script from the app directory. It starts the Vite dev server itself.
   ```
   node .claude/skills/verify-render/scripts/verify-render.mjs --root <app dir> [--state <name>]
   ```
   It writes `shots/<state>.png` under the app dir and prints one line per check. Exit code is
   non-zero if any check fails or any state fails to render.
2. **Read every screenshot** with the Read tool. For each, compare the frame against the
   state's `describe()` line printed above it. Decide: does the picture show what the line
   says? Numbers catch overlap; only eyes catch "the stone is on the wrong side of the wheel".
3. Report in three groups: numeric failures (quote the detail line), visual disagreements
   (name the frame and what is off), and frames that pass both. A state passes only when both
   agree.
4. Fix in the sim or shapes, never by editing a check's tolerance or a state's expectation to
   match the picture. If an expectation was genuinely wrong, say so in the transcript and
   change it in `states.ts` with a one-line comment giving the reason.

Done when every state passes both the numbers and your eyes, or the remaining failures are
listed with a cause for each.
verify-render.mjs
// Screenshot every named state of the app and run its numeric checks. See ../SKILL.md.
import { chromium } from "playwright";
import { createServer } from "vite";
import { mkdirSync } from "node:fs";
import { resolve } from "node:path";

const args = process.argv.slice(2);
const opt = (flag, dflt) => { const i = args.indexOf(flag); return i >= 0 ? args[i + 1] : dflt; };
const root = resolve(opt("--root", process.cwd()));
const only = opt("--state", null);
const port = Number(opt("--port", 5199));
const viewport = { width: Number(opt("--width", 900)), height: Number(opt("--height", 900)) };

mkdirSync(resolve(root, "shots"), { recursive: true });
const server = await createServer({ root, server: { port, strictPort: true }, logLevel: "silent" });
await server.listen();
const browser = await chromium.launch();
const page = await browser.newPage({ viewport });
const errors = [];
page.on("pageerror", (e) => errors.push(String(e)));

let failed = 0;
try {
  await page.goto(`http://localhost:${port}/`);
  await page.waitForFunction(() => window.__bench?.states, null, { timeout: 10000 });
  const states = await page.evaluate(() => window.__bench.states());
  const wanted = only ? states.filter((s) => s === only) : states;
  if (only && wanted.length === 0) { console.error(`no state named ${only}; have: ${states.join(", ")}`); process.exit(2); }
  for (const name of wanted) {
    await page.goto(`http://localhost:${port}/?state=${encodeURIComponent(name)}`);
    await page.waitForSelector(`svg[data-state="${name}"]`, { timeout: 10000 });
    const file = resolve(root, "shots", `${name}.png`);
    await page.screenshot({ path: file });
    const describe = await page.evaluate(() => window.__bench.describe());
    const checks = await page.evaluate(() => window.__bench.check());
    const bad = checks.filter((c) => !c.pass);
    failed += bad.length;
    console.log(`\n${bad.length ? "✗" : "✓"} ${name} — ${describe}\n  ${file}`);
    for (const c of checks) console.log(`  ${c.pass ? "ok  " : "FAIL"} ${c.name}: ${c.detail}`);
  }
} catch (e) {
  console.error(String(e));
  failed++;
} finally {
  if (errors.length) { console.error("\npage errors:\n" + errors.join("\n")); failed++; }
  await browser.close();
  await server.close();
}
console.log(`\n${failed ? `${failed} failure(s)` : "all states pass numeric checks"}; now read the screenshots.`);
process.exit(failed ? 1 : 0);
{
  "name": "watchmakers-bench",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "tsc --noEmit -p . && vite build",
    "preview": "vite preview",
    "test": "vitest run"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "typescript": "^5.6.0",
    "vite": "^6.0.0",
    "vitest": "^3.0.0",
    "playwright": "^1.50.0"
  }
}

# Beat rates and how a timegrapher reads a movement

Research note for The Watchmaker's Bench, 2026-11-01. Sources read directly: the `tg` open-source timegrapher source (vacaboja), Witschi product leaflets and the WisioScope product page, ETA's CT 2824-2 technical communication, Ciechanowski's *Mechanical Watch*, Wikipedia (ETA SA, Lever escapement), Caliber Corner, Watchguy's lift-angle table, and WatchRepairTalk threads. Claims are tagged **[verified]** (read in a primary or owning source), **[secondary]** (plausible, only seen second-hand), or **[unverified]**.

## (a) Beat rates, beat period, balance frequency

One **beat** (also "vibration", "alternance", French *alternance*, hence ETA's "A/h" or "alt/h") is one half-swing of the balance, from one extreme to the other. Each half-swing releases one escape-wheel tooth and makes one tick. One full oscillation is two beats. **[verified]** Ciechanowski: "the balance wheel does a full back-and-forth swing four times per second, hitting the pallet fork twice during each cycle, for a total of 8 beats per second or 28,800 beats per hour." ETA's CT 2824-2 lists "Fréquence 28'800 alt/h" and "Typical angle lift of balance 50°".

| bph | beat period (s) | oscillation period T (s) | balance frequency (Hz) | beats per day |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 18,000 | 0.2000 | 0.4000 | 2.5 | 432,000 |
| 19,800 | 0.1818 | 0.3636 | 2.75 | 475,200 |
| 21,600 | 0.1667 | 0.3333 | 3.0 | 518,400 |
| 25,200 | 0.1429 | 0.2857 | 3.5 | 604,800 |
| 28,800 | 0.1250 | 0.2500 | 4.0 | 691,200 |
| 36,000 | 0.1000 | 0.2000 | 5.0 | 864,000 |

Formulas: beat period = 3600 / bph; T = 7200 / bph; f = bph / 7200. **[verified]** by arithmetic and matched to `tg` (`compute_period` searches around `7200 * sample_rate / bph`, so `tg`'s internal "period" is the full oscillation, two beats). `tg` presets exactly this list plus 12,000, 14,400, 17,280, 43,200 and 72,000 bph; Witschi instruments accept 3,600 to 72,000 A/h. **[verified]**

## (b) How the timegrapher derives rate, beat error and amplitude

**Rate.** The machine measures the actual tick-to-tick interval against the nominal one for the selected beat rate and scales the fractional error to a day. In `tg` (`computer.c`): `rate = (7200 / (bph * T_measured) - 1) * 24 * 3600` s/day, where `T_measured` is the measured two-beat period in seconds. Equivalent: rate = (T_nominal / T_measured − 1) × 86,400. Positive means the watch runs fast. **[verified, tg source]** The sensitivity is tiny per beat: 10 s/day at 28,800 bph is 14.5 µs per beat, so machines average many beats before displaying. Witschi quotes ±0.1 s/d accuracy with ranges of ±999 s/d. **[verified, Witschi X1 leaflet]** The lift angle setting does not affect rate. **[verified, tg source; secondary on forums]**

**Beat error.** With a beat error the tick→tock interval d1 and tock→tick interval d2 are unequal. `tg` computes `be = T/2 - d1` (`algo.c` `compute_parameters`), reported as |be| in ms. Since d2 = T − d1, this equals |d2 − d1| / 2, which is also exactly the horizontal separation of the two trace lines. **[verified, tg source]** Whether Witschi and Weishi report the half-difference (trace separation) or the full difference |d2 − d1| I could not confirm from a Witschi manual; forum and vendor guides only say "the difference between tic and toc". **[unverified; see recommendation below]** Range on every machine is 0 to 9.9 ms, resolution 0.1 ms. **[verified, Witschi leaflets; Weishi manual via search snippet, secondary]**

**Amplitude.** Acoustic machines cannot see the balance, so they time how long the balance takes to cross the lift angle, the arc over which the impulse pin is engaged with the pallet fork. Witschi's explanation, quoted on WatchRepairTalk: "To calculate the amplitude, the time between the first pulse and the third pulse of the beat noise is measured. Between these two pulses, the balance wheel rotates a certain angle. This so-called lift angle is determined by the construction of the movement and is entered as a parameter. The larger the amplitude ... the shorter is the time it needs to traverse this angle." **[secondary, forum quote attributed to Witschi]** Witschi's own WisioScope page confirms the principle by contrast: an optical sensor gives "actual amplitude, independent of lift angle". **[verified]**

The formula, from simple harmonic motion θ(t) = A·sin(2πt/T) with the lift angle λ centred on the rest position, is:

    A = (λ / 2) / sin(π · Δt / T)

where Δt is the unlock-to-lock interval within one beat and T is the full oscillation period (two beats). This is exactly what `tg` implements: `amp = la * 0.5 / sin(M_PI * pulse / period)` (`algo.c` `compute_amplitude`), and the inverse `asin(lift_angle / (2 * amp)) / M_PI` in `output_panel.c`. `tg` only accepts a result if both tick and tock give 135° to 360° and agree within 60°. **[verified, tg source]** The formula in the task brief, `lift_angle / (2π·Δt/T)`, is the small-angle approximation of this and is wrong by a few percent at normal amplitudes; use the sine form. Worked values at λ = 52°: 28,800 bph, A = 280° gives Δt = 7.4 ms; A = 200° gives 10.4 ms; 18,000 bph, A = 280° gives 11.8 ms. The reported amplitude is the half-amplitude: the swing from the rest position to one extreme, so "280°" means 280° each way. **[secondary, Watchguy comment; consistent with the formula]**

**Why 52°.** It is the long-standing default on timing machines (`tg` `DEFAULT_LA 52`; the Weishi 1000 manual says "factory set it to 52°", range 30° to 70°; Caliber Corner: "52° is a generally assumed average and also the default lift angle on most timing machines", most calibres fall "between 48-54 degrees"). **[verified for tg; secondary for Weishi and the "why"]** Real values differ by calibre. ETA states 50° for the 2824-2. **[verified, ETA CT 2824-2, 2011 and 2022 editions]** Watchguy's table lists ETA 2824 53°, 2892-A2 52°, 7750 49°, 6497 44°, Seiko 7S26/4R36 53°, Rolex 3135 52°, Unitas 52°. **[secondary, community table]** Amplitude reads linearly in λ, so a 1° error in the setting is about a 2% error in amplitude. Caliber Corner's example (52° vs 51° taking a reading from 239° to 228°) is larger than that and I could not reconcile it. **[unverified]** Witschi machines accept 10° to 90°. **[verified]**

## (c) What the trace shows

Each tick is plotted as one dot. The horizontal position (on a vertical strip like `tg`'s, or the vertical position on the horizontal Witschi/Weishi display) is the tick's time offset measured modulo the nominal beat period; successive beats advance by one row. If the watch runs exactly on time every dot lands in the same column. If it runs fast, each tick arrives slightly early and the dots drift, so the line's slope is the rate. In `tg`: `slope = -rate * zoom / 86400` in units of strip width per beat, with strip width = beat period / 10 (12.5 ms at 28,800 bph, 20 ms at 18,000), and a horizontal guide line every 10 s. **[verified, tg `output_panel.c`, `PAPERSTRIP_ZOOM 10`]** Ticks and tocks alternate, so with beat error the odd and even dots form two parallel lines separated by the beat error in ms; a single clean line means near-zero beat error. **[verified in tg; secondary for Witschi/Weishi]** Witschi's Watch Expert III leaflet gives the display scale as "Time scale adjustable from 1 up to 9 mm / ms (zoom)" on a 256 × 64-dot screen, and the Weishi 1900 display is 480 dots wide; so one screen is a few hundred beats, roughly 10 to 60 s of ticking. **[verified for Witschi; secondary for Weishi]** Scatter in the dots means an unstable escapement; two lines with different slopes do not occur in a healthy movement.

## (d) The sounds of one Swiss lever beat

Witschi's amplitude method implies three audible pulses per beat: (1) **unlocking**, the impulse pin hits the fork and the pallet stone slides off the escape-wheel tooth against the draw; (2) **impulse**, the tooth slides down the pallet's impulse plane and pushes the balance; (3) **drop/lock**, the escape wheel drops and the next tooth lands on the locking face of the other pallet while the lever hits the banking pin. The WatchRepairTalk quote attributes the measured pulses to "the escape-wheel tooth meeting the locking plane of the pallet-stone and the lever hitting the banking-pin". **[secondary]** The lever escapement phases themselves (unlock, impulse, drop, lock, with draw holding the lever on the banking) are standard. **[verified, Wikipedia Lever escapement; Ciechanowski's step list "escape wheel unlocks ... pallet fork pushes the jewel roller ... escape wheel locks again"]** Timing: pulse 1 to pulse 3 is the lift-angle traverse, Δt in the formula above, so about 7 to 12 ms at 280° depending on beat rate, and longer at lower amplitude. `tg` searches for pulse 1 up to one eighth of a period (31 ms at 28,800 bph) before the loudest pulse and treats the loudest pulse as the lock. **[verified, tg source]** The relative loudness and the position of the impulse pulse between the two I could not verify from a primary source. **[unverified]**

## (e) Tolerances

- ETA 2824-2 grades, mean rate and max positional variation: Standard, 2 positions, ±12 s/d, variation ±30; Elaboré, 3 positions, ±7 s/d, variation ±20; Top, 5 positions, ±4 s/d, variation ±15; Chronometer follows COSC (−4/+6 s/d mean daily rate). **[secondary, Wikipedia ETA SA; ETA's own manufacturing-information sheet with amplitude and beat-error limits was not found online]**
- Beat error: vendor and watchmaker guides treat under about 0.5 to 0.6 ms as good; ETA's own figure not found. Forum readings on a freshly serviced 2824-2 show 0.1 ms. **[secondary]**
- Amplitude: Caliber Corner quotes 260° to 310° for a healthy movement at full wind, dial up, falling as oils age; forum readings on a serviced 2824-2 show 278° to 286°. Vertical positions read lower than dial up. **[secondary]** Machines refuse readings below 70° to 80° (Witschi) or 135° (`tg`). **[verified]**
- Measurement precision of the instruments: rate ±0.1 s/d, amplitude ±0.4° to ±1°, beat error ±0.1 ms. **[verified, Witschi leaflets]**

## Numbers and formulas to use in the simulation

| Item | Recommendation | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Beat definition | 1 beat = 1 half-swing = 1 tick; beat period = 3600/bph; T = 7200/bph | High (verified) |
| Default calibre beat rate | 28,800 bph (4 Hz), optional second calibre 18,000 bph (2.5 Hz) | High |
| Rate | `rate_s_per_day = (T_nominal / T_measured - 1) * 86400`, average over many beats; + = fast | High (tg source) |
| Beat error | Display `abs(d2 - d1) / 2` in ms (equals the trace-line separation, matches tg); note in GLOSSARY that some machines may show the full difference | Medium (tg verified; Witschi convention unverified) |
| Amplitude | `A = (lift / 2) / sin(pi * dt / T)` where dt = unlock-to-lock time; invert to produce dt from the simulated amplitude | High (tg source, SHM derivation) |
| Lift angle | Parameter per calibre; machine default 52°, sim calibre 50° for an ETA 2824-2-like movement, 44° for a 6497-like pocket calibre | High for 52° default and ETA 50°; Medium for others |
| Healthy amplitude | 270° to 300° dial up at full wind; below 200° is a fault; trace invalid below 135° | Medium (secondary only) |
| Healthy rate / beat error | Within ±10 s/d and under 0.5 ms as "healthy"; ±12 s/d ETA Standard; puzzle "runs fast" at +40 s/d is clearly out of spec | Medium |
| Trace geometry | One dot per beat, x = tick offset mod beat period, slope ∝ rate, two lines separated by beat error; show about 300 beats per screen (about 37 s at 28,800 bph) | High for the mechanism; Medium for the screen scale |
| Beat sounds | Three pulses per beat: unlock, impulse, lock; pulse 1 to pulse 3 spans the lift angle (7 to 12 ms at 280°) | Medium (Witschi description is second-hand) |

Sources: `tg` source files `algo.c`, `computer.c`, `output_panel.c`, `tg.h` at https://github.com/vacaboja/tg ; Witschi Watch Expert III leaflet (cousinsuk.com/PDF/skus/643_leaflet_watchexpertIII t20214.pdf), Chronoscope X1 leaflet (cousinsuk.com/PDF/skus/3531_T32439_leaflet_chronoscope-X1 (G2).pdf), WisioScope page https://www.witschi.com/en/?p=2757 ; ETA CT 2824-2 https://shopb2b.eta.ch/technicaldocuments/index/pdf/id/1883 and /1884 ; https://ciechanow.ski/mechanical-watch/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ETA_SA ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lever_escapement ; https://calibercorner.com/lift-angle/ ; https://calibercorner.com/amplitude/ ; https://watchguy.co.uk/cgi-bin/lift_angles ; https://watchguy.co.uk/?p=2502 ; https://www.watchrepairtalk.com/topic/2727-how-does-the-timegrapheror-vibrograph-measure-amplitude/ ; Weishi 1000 manual (manuals.online, via search snippet only).

1-# 04 Positional error: positions, pivot friction, poise
2-
3:Researched 2026-11-01 for the Watchmaker's Bench sim. Scope: (a) the standard positions and why horizontal and vertical differ, (b) poise error and the "220° rule", (c) magnitudes, (d) a formula the sim can use.
4-
5-Confidence labels: **[P]** verified from a primary source (standard, manufacturer document, patent citing the horological literature); **[S]** plausible, secondary only (blogs, forum practitioners); **[U]** could not verify.
6-
7-## (a) Positions and why horizontal differs from vertical
--
9-**Vocabulary [P].** Witschi's *Testing of mechanical watches* (2025 PDF, p. 21) lists the six industry positions: dial up (CH), dial down (CB), crown down (9H), crown left (6H), crown up (3H), crown right (12H). The `nH` code names the hour index that sits at the **top**: the Rolex patent US10120341B2 defines 12H as "the index 12H of the dial ... situated at the top relative to the vector g" and 3H as "with the movement shaft at the top", citing NIHS notation and *Traité de construction horlogère* p. 741. ISO 3159 / COSC use five of these: 6H, 3H, 9H, FH (fond haut = dial down, Witschi's CB) and CH; 12H (crown right) is not tested (COSC: "tested in 5 positions"; Wikipedia lists "3 o'clock, 6 o'clock, 9 o'clock, dial on top, dial on the bottom"). Note Witschi's own p. 27 calls 6H "crown down", contradicting its p. 21 and the patent; treat 6H = crown left, 9H = crown down.
10-
11:**Why vertical is worse [P for mechanism, S for the numbers].** Witschi p. 21 gives three reasons for multi-position testing: gravity acting on balance and escapement, imbalance of the balance, and "friction in the balance bearings varies with the position of the watch, leading to changes in both amplitude and rate". SJX (Richard Lee and Ashton Tracy, 2020) describe the geometry: dial up/down "has the least friction, with the main contact being the tip of the lower pivot ... akin to a spinning top on a table", while on its side "both pivots [are] turning against the wall of the bearings ... akin to a pen being laid flat", so "friction on the pivots will always be higher when the watch is placed on its side" and the visible symptom is "a drop in amplitude".
12-
13-**Size of the amplitude drop.** Witschi's worked six-position dataset (p. 26) is a real-looking example: fully wound CH 298°, CB 294°, vertical 278–287°; after 24 h horizontal 286–298°, vertical 264–279°. Its DVH amplitude value is −12° at 0 h **[P, one example]**. Practitioner consensus on watchrepairtalk is "around 30° (±10°)" for wristwatches, ~40° for slow-beat vintage, ~60° for Unitas 6498 pocket calibres; drops near 100° indicate a fault (pivot ends polished too round, excess lock) **[S]**. Witschi p. 12: healthy full-wind amplitude 270–310°, lift angle ≈ 51° for most modern movements **[P]**.
14-
15:## (b) Poise error and the 220° rule
16-
17:**What it is [P].** The Rolex patent defines static imbalance as "the product of the mass of the balance times the distance between its center of gravity and the axis of rotation ... typically measured in µg·cm or nN·m. With terrestrial gravity, 1 µg·cm corresponds to approximately 0.1 nN·m." It states, citing J.-J. Augsburger, *La mise d'équilibre des balanciers*, Proc. Swiss Chronometry Congress 1966 p. 324: the rate effect "is proportional to the imbalance itself", "inversely proportional to the inertia of the balance", "highly dependent on the amplitude of oscillation ... It is even cancelled out completely for an amplitude close to 220°", "varies as the sine of the azimuth angle between the axis of the balance ... and the vertical" (so zero when dial up/down) and "varies with the angle between the direction of the imbalance and the vertical", with two opposite vertical positions where it vanishes and two, 90° away, where it is maximal. A second zero exists near 400° (patent, description).
18-
19:**Why 220° [P, derivation checked here].** Put the heavy spot at angle φ from the downward vertical when the balance is at rest (φ = 0: heavy spot at the bottom). Gravity adds the torque −g·u·cos φ·sin θ to the hairspring's −k·θ (u = mass × eccentricity; the sin φ part only shifts the rest position and is second order). Harmonic balance of sin(Θ cos ωt) gives a fundamental 2J1(Θ)cos ωt, so
20-
21-    ω² = ω0² · [1 + (g·u·cos φ / (I·ω0²)) · 2·J1(Θ)/Θ]
22-    rate [s/d] ≈ 86400 · (g · u · cos φ / (I · ω0²)) · J1(Θ)/Θ
23-
24:with I the balance inertia, ω0 = 2πf, Θ the amplitude in radians (zero to turning point, the timegrapher convention). J1's first zero is 3.8317 rad = **219.54°**, which is the 220° rule. The patent's claim 9 is exactly the least-squares inverse of this expression: `3H(θ) − 9H(θ) = 2·86400·g·bx /(I·(2πf)²) · J1(θ)/θ`, with x the 9H direction, so the model and the primary source agree on form and on the (2πf)² factor.
25-
26:**Sign [P via patent axes, S via practitioners].** In the patent, bx > 0 (heavy spot toward the 9H index) makes 3H(θ) − 9H(θ) positive for Θ < 220°; in position 3H the 9H index is at the bottom. Hence: **heavy spot at the bottom at rest, amplitude below 220° → the watch gains; above 220° → it loses; heavy spot at the top is the mirror image.** Practitioners state the same: "influence is zero at about 220 degrees, and it changes from fast to slow under and over 220 deg", and the Greiner dynamic-poising procedure (Mark, watchrepairtalk, 19 Dec 2014) tests at 150–180° and takes the fastest vertical position as the one with the heavy spot down. Physical picture (forum, [S]): at low amplitude the heavy spot stays near the bottom and gravity stiffens the restoring torque like a pendulum; above 220° it spends enough of each swing past the horizontal that the net effect reverses.
27-
28:**Dynamic poising at one amplitude is unreliable [P].** The patent, quoting Vermot et al. *Traité de construction horlogère* (PPUR 2011, pp. 190–200), warns that single-amplitude "rate to positions" poising "lacks precision" because other position errors (hairspring, escapement) are mixed in; Rolex's method fits the J1 curve across amplitudes either side of 220°. A side note: WO2012007460 recommends correcting at 137° or 316.5° (the zeros of J0) so the material removed does not itself unbalance; that is a manufacturing detail, not a rate rule **[U, not pursued]**.
29-

A 10 µg·cm fault at full wind therefore reads as a 10–15 s/d spread between opposite vertical positions, which matches the patent's "±7 s/d" example in scale.

67-## Sources

1-# 03 — Balance amplitude and isochronism
2-
3:Research note for The Watchmaker's Bench. Date: 2026-11-01. Scope: (a) how amplitude follows mainspring torque, (b) why amplitude changes rate in a Swiss lever watch and in which direction, (c) other isochronism effects (hairspring, regulator pins, overcoil, knocking), (d) an analytic model to encode. Each claim is tagged **[V]** verified from a primary source, **[P]** plausible but secondary/forum only, or **[X]** could not verify.
4-
5-## Sources actually read
6-
7-- Airy, G. B., "On the Disturbances of Pendulums and Balances, and on the Theory of Escapements", Trans. Cambridge Phil. Soc. III (read 1826, printed 1830). Transcription: https://theindex.nawcc.org/Articles/AiryOnPendulumsAndBalanceWheels.htm ; annotated PDF by D. Roegel: https://members.loria.fr/Roegel/loc/airy1827annotated.pdf
--
30-- **Modern form.** [V] Hoyng Eq. 10: rate − 1 = −λ²/16 − (1/λ)∮ m sinψ dψ; the second term "is called the escapement error ... as computed already by Airy". For a single impulse of energy e at phase ψ₁ (Eq. 29–30): escapement error = −(e / 2πλ²)·tan ψ₁, which "either increases the rate (ψ₁ < 0, impulse before a zero), or reduces it (ψ₁ > 0, impulse after a zero)". Note the 1/λ² and tan ψ₁ = φ₁/√(λ²−φ₁²): a fixed impulse angle φ₁ matters more as amplitude λ shrinks.
31-- **Applied to the Swiss lever.** [V] US 9,323,223 (industry patent): the oscillator "is subjected to a resistant torque before the line of centres, and this causes a loss"; then "a drive torque firstly before the line of centres, which causes a gain, then after the line of centres, which causes a loss"; "the escapement thus produces a rate loss and this disturbance caused by the escapement is greater for small oscillation amplitudes". SJX (Dec 2025) gives the same phase-by-phase account: unlocking → loss; impulse before equilibrium → gain; impulse after equilibrium and the run to banking → loss; net loss. Stoimenov: the lever engages over about ±15° of a ±270° swing, so the balance is free for >88% of the period [V].
32:- **So which way does a real watch go?** The *escapement alone* makes a Swiss lever watch **lose more as amplitude falls** [V, three independent sources]. But bench experience often shows the opposite net sign: "the movement works faster in the end of power reserve, when the amplitude is smaller" (nevenbekriev), "if the rate is higher when the amplitude is lower ... check the hairspring is centred in the regulator pins" (Klassiker), "at very low amplitudes the rate can increase considerably" [P]. The gain comes from the hairspring/regulator-pin system (section c), which is deliberately set to over-compensate the escapement loss. The patent quantifies the compensation designers aim for: a hairspring-induced gain "of at least 2 s/d, or at least 4 s/d, or even at least 6 s/d, or even at least 8 s/d, at an amplitude of 150° with respect to an amplitude of 300°" [V]. Witschi's worked example (0 h vs 24 h) shows gains of +1.7 and +2.9 s/d where amplitude fell 8° and 23° and essentially no change where amplitude did not fall [V, but an illustrative dataset].
33-- **Magnitude.** [P] Escapement-only loss: order 2–8 s/d over a 150° amplitude drop, i.e. roughly 0.1–0.5 s/d per 10°, growing as amplitude falls. Net, pin-compensated watch: typically ±1 s/d per 10° over the 240–300° band (Witschi example, Ie values of a few s/d). Pathological pin contact: −53 → −19.3 s/d as amplitude fell 249° → 204° (Seiko Marvel case, ≈ +7 s/d per 10°) [P]. No source gives a single universal coefficient [X].
34-
35-## (c) Other isochronism effects
36-
37:- **Regulator pins (flat spring).** [P, consistent across watchmakers] With the spring centred and a correct gap, at very low amplitude the spring is free between the pins (full length → slow), at higher amplitude it touches the pins more (shorter effective length → faster), averaging out over the normal band (JohnR725). If the spring rests against one pin, the watch "runs fast at low amplitudes" and slows as amplitude lifts it off (JohnR725, nevenbekriev). Opening the gap "will slow the rate, more so for low amplitudes" (Klassiker). Witschi lists "clearance in the regulator pins" among the main isochronism factors [V]. US 7,648,265 (via search): "depending on the distance of the regulator pins, oscillations at small amplitudes can be speeded up or slowed down" [P].
38:- **Pinning point / stud, Breguet overcoil.** [V] A flat spring with a fixed outer pinning point cannot "breathe" concentrically; the eccentric development loads the pivots and disturbs isochronism (SJX overcoil article; Wikipedia citing Phillips 1861, who proved a spring whose centre of gravity stays on the balance axis is isochronous). The overcoil raises the last coil and curves it toward the pinning point so the body develops concentrically; Phillips' conditions fix the end-curve's centre of gravity. [P] With an overcoil, "the overcoil is calculated to be isochronous"; residual error is corrected by reshaping it: closer to the balance centre raises the rate at low amplitude, further out lowers it (nickelsilver). Overcoil watches also need a pin-free or wide-pin regulator, which is why they hold rate 0 h→24 h despite a 40° drop (nickelsilver, same post).
39-- **Hairspring quality / material.** [P] Steel springs: centrifugal effect on balance arms slows the rate at high amplitude while less pin contact raises it, partly compensating (nickelsilver). Modern Nivarox-class alloys remove most of this.
40-- **Knocking / rebanking at very high amplitude.** [V] Horopedia: beyond ~280–300° (lift-angle dependent) "a knock (rebate) phenomenon causes the oscillator to run away and results in an exaggerated advance". [P] Mechanism: the impulse pin strikes the outside of the fork horn (the lever is against its banking pin) and bounces back early, truncating the swing → shorter period → sudden large gain, with a "galloping" sound; timegrapher traces go chaotic and reported amplitude becomes meaningless. Thresholds quoted: ~320–330° at full wind for a modern 51–52° lift-angle calibre; Omega guidance quoted as <315° dial-up automatic, <325° manual; a Raketa case shows disorder "as soon as the amplitude reaches near 325 degrees"; overbanking (pin stuck behind the horn) needs ~350°. Causes: too strong a mainspring, fresh lubrication, dial-up position [P].
41-
42-## (d) Analytic model used in the literature

/**
 * The instrument. Reads a window of ticks and reports what a bench timegrapher reports.
 * Formulas per docs/research/02-beat-rates-and-timegrapher.md (verified against the `tg`
 * open-source timegrapher):
 *   rate  = (T_nominal / T_measured − 1) · 86400          (+ = fast)
 *   beat error = |d2 − d1| / 2                             (equals trace-line separation)
 *   amplitude = (lift / 2) / sin(π · dt / T)               (dt = unlock-to-lock time)
 */
import type { Tick } from "../oscillator/ticks";

export interface Reading {
  rateSecondsPerDay: number;
  beatErrorMs: number;
  amplitudeDeg: number;
  /** One point per tick: beat index and the tick's offset from the nominal grid, ms. */
  trace: { beat: number; offsetMs: number; parity: 0 | 1 }[];
  beats: number;
}

export function analyze(ticks: Tick[], nominalPeriod: number, liftAngleDeg: number): Reading | null {
  if (ticks.length < 4) return null;
  const beat = nominalPeriod / 2;
  const n = ticks.length;
  // Measured period from first and last tick of matching parity (whole periods between them).
  const lastSame = n - 1 - ((n - 1) % 2);
  const periods = lastSame / 2;
  const measuredPeriod = (ticks[lastSame].t - ticks[0].t) / periods;
  const rateSecondsPerDay = (nominalPeriod / measuredPeriod - 1) * 86400;

  let d1 = 0, d2 = 0, c1 = 0, c2 = 0;
  for (let i = 1; i < n; i++) {
    const d = ticks[i].t - ticks[i - 1].t;
    if (ticks[i - 1].parity === 0) { d1 += d; c1++; } else { d2 += d; c2++; }
  }
  const beatErrorMs = c1 && c2 ? (Math.abs(d2 / c2 - d1 / c1) / 2) * 1000 : 0;

  const dt = ticks.reduce((a, k) => a + k.liftDuration, 0) / n;
  const amplitudeDeg = liftAngleDeg / 2 / Math.sin((Math.PI * dt) / measuredPeriod);

  const trace = ticks.map((k, i) => ({ beat: i, offsetMs: (k.t - ticks[0].t - i * beat) * 1000, parity: k.parity }));
  return { rateSecondsPerDay, beatErrorMs, amplitudeDeg, trace, beats: n };
}

    <summary>How to read the trace</summary>
    <p>Each dot is one tick. The screen holds about a minute of ticks.</p>
    <dl>
      <dt>Flat line</dt><dd>The watch keeps time.</dd>
      <dt>Sloping line</dt><dd>The watch is gaining or losing. Here, down to the right means gaining. Steeper is worse.</dd>
      <dt>Two lines apart</dt><dd>Out of beat: the tick and the tock are not evenly spaced.</dd>
    </dl>
    <p>Below the screen, three numbers.</p>
    <dl>
      <dt>rate</dt><dd>Seconds gained (+) or lost (−) per day. Zero is perfect.</dd>
      <dt>amplitude</dt><dd>How far the balance swings each way, in degrees. Healthy is about 250 to 300.</dd>
      <dt>beat error</dt><dd>How uneven tick and tock are, in milliseconds. Under 0.5 is good.</dd>
    </dl>
  </details>
  <div class="hint" hidden></div>`;

export function mountOnboarding(): void {
  const sheet = document.querySelector(".sheet");
  const main = document.querySelector("main");
  const puzzleEl = document.getElementById("puzzle");
  if (!sheet || !main || !puzzleEl) return;

  const forced = FORCED[new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("state") ?? ""];
  const anyNamedState = new URLSearchParams(location.search).has("state");
  // Design's named states must screenshot without this layer; only onboarding's own states show it.
  if (anyNamedState && !forced) return;

  document.head.appendChild(Object.assign(document.createElement("style"), { textContent: STYLE }));

  // First-run strip, between the title block and the two pictures. Never covers the controls.
  const strip = document.createElement("section");
  strip.id = "onboarding";
  strip.setAttribute("aria-label", "First-run guide");
  strip.innerHTML = FIRST_RUN;
  main.before(strip);

  // Always-available explainer plus the hint slot, under the job card.
  const help = document.createElement("aside");
  help.id = "bench-help";
  help.innerHTML = TRACE_EXPLAINER;
  puzzleEl.after(help);
  const details = help.querySelector("details")!;
  const hintEl = help.querySelector<HTMLElement>(".hint")!;

  let dismissed = false;
  try { dismissed = localStorage.getItem(DISMISS_KEY) === "1"; } catch { /* private mode: no persistence */ }
  if (forced) dismissed = forced !== "first-run";
  strip.hidden = dismissed;

  strip.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('[data-act="dismiss"]')!.onclick = () => {
    strip.hidden = true;
    try { localStorage.setItem(DISMISS_KEY, "1"); } catch { /* ignore */ }
  };
  strip.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('[data-act="trace"]')!.onclick = () => {
    details.open = true;
    details.scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth", block: "nearest" });
  };

  // Progressive hint: one per puzzle, after 60 wall-seconds without the hold bar moving or an answer chosen.
  const select = document.getElementById("puzzle-select") as HTMLSelectElement | null;
  let puzzleId = select?.value ?? "";
  let since = performance.now();
  const showHint = (id: string) => {
    const text = HINTS[id];
    if (!text) return;
    hintEl.innerHTML = `<span class="tag">Hint</span>${text}`;
    hintEl.hidden = false;
  };
  const progressed = () => {
    const bar = puzzleEl.querySelector(".hold span")?.textContent ?? "";
    if (bar && !bar.startsWith("0 /")) return true;
    if (puzzleEl.querySelector(".choice.right, .choice.wrong")) return true;
    return false;
  };
  const tick = () => {
    const now = select?.value ?? "";
    if (now !== puzzleId) { puzzleId = now; since = performance.now(); hintEl.hidden = true; }
    if (!hintEl.hidden || !puzzleId) return;
    if (progressed()) { since = performance.now(); return; }
    if (performance.now() - since >= HINT_AFTER_MS) showHint(puzzleId);
  };

  if (forced === "trace") details.open = true;
  if (forced === "hint") showHint(puzzleId);
  if (!forced) setInterval(tick, 1000);
}

git -C .claude/worktrees/onboarding diff HEAD > /tmp/onboarding.patch && git apply /tmp/onboarding.patch && cp .claude/worktrees/onboarding/src/app/onboarding.ts src/app/ && cp .claude/worktrees/onboarding/scripts/onboarding-e2e.mjs scripts/

What a newcomer sees in the first 30 seconds. Under the title block, a strip headed "First time at the bench? Three things to know" with three numbered items. One: left is the movement, the tick-tock engine, the big ring is the balance. Two: right is the timegrapher, the instrument a watchmaker listens with, and rate means seconds gained or lost per day. Three: the job is on the card, move one slider at the bottom, you are winning when the bar fills. Two buttons sit beside the heading: "How do I read the screen?" opens the explainer in place, "Got it" hides the strip and remembers that in localStorage. Below, the job card now says "Slide Regulator index toward S (slow) until rate reads between −5 and +5 s/day". At 1280×900 the goal and the hold bar are on screen. Named states used by design do not show the strip, so their screenshots are unchanged.

The explainer is reachable any time from the strip: each dot is one tick; flat line keeps time; sloping line gains or loses, and on this screen down to the right means gaining; two lines apart means out of beat; then the three numbers with healthy values.

Hints appear after 60 wall-seconds without the hold bar moving or an answer chosen, one per puzzle, naming the control and the number to watch.

Strings I was unsure of, not shipped blindly: - "Here, down to the right means gaining." I checked the sign in the analyzer and the view: early ticks give negative offsets, which the view draws lower. If design flips the vertical axis this sentence becomes wrong. - Puzzle 3's explanation says a smaller swing runs faster "because the regulator pins touch the spring differently; the escapement alone would make it lose, but the pins win." Research note 03 marks the pin mechanism as plausible but secondary and says to phrase it as typical of flat-spring watches, which the card does with "a watch like this one". - Puzzle 4's hint tells the user the heavy spot is at the bottom when crown up and to remove about 10 µg·cm at 0°. That gives the answer away, which I judged right for a hint that only fires after a minute of no progress. - The puzzle 4 goal says "within 3 s/day of dial up", but the completion rule checks residual unbalance, not rate. The two agree at this amplitude, and the bar can also fill while the watch sits dial up.

Screenshots are in .claude/worktrees/onboarding/shots/: onboarding-first-run.png, onboarding-trace-explainer.png, onboarding-hint.png, plus onboarding-live-desktop-900.png, onboarding-live-hint.png and onboarding-live-mobile.png from the live run.

Left for others. The control row is still below the fold at 1280×900; I asked design in the handoffs file to consider a shorter movement panel or a sticky footer. The wrong-answer verdict for puzzle 3 is hard-coded in main.ts, which physics owns, so I asked for a whyWrong field.

result: Onboarding layer, beginner puzzle copy, 60-second hints and three named states built and verified in worktree onboarding, uncommitted as instructed.
